As sensors and controllers proliferate throughout building management systems, traffic networks, and power grids, the diverse ecosystem of devices creates significant challenges due to varying communication protocols, data formats, and controllability features. To establish a foundation for productive cross-sector dialogue, three speakers presented on the current state of legacy devices in transportation, grid, and building systems. These presentations provided essential context about sector- specific challenges, existing infrastructure constraints, and emerging solutions before participants engaged in the workshop’s primary focus: interactive breakout sessions designed to identify specific legacy devices, transferable strategies and uncover common patterns across different domains. This section summarizes the foundational presen- tations from Session 1, while the remainder of this report synthesizes the insights and conclusions drawn from the breakout group discussions and plenary session conducted in Sessions 2 and 3. 1.2 Workshop Agenda Figure1.LegacyDevicesWorkshopAgenda 1.3 Summary of Workshop Presentations 1.3.1 “Works in Theory”: Mobility Angle(Jibonananda Sanyal, NLR) In this presentation, Jibo Sanyal from NLR’s Energy Conversion and Storage Systems center presented on build- ing observability at scale for urban mobility systems, focusing on the challenges and opportunities presented by legacy transportation infrastructure. Sanyal outlined the CTwin project–a "Digital Twin" (AMPO 2021) for regional mobility in Chattanooga, Tennessee–which demonstrates how real-time data feeds can be integrated with simula- tion, modeling, and machine learning to create situational awareness and enable cyber-physical control actions at a regional scale (Sanyal 2020). 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications The CTwin system aggregates over 500 primary data streams from seven proprietary vendor systems across three institutions, including data from the Chattanooga, Tennessee, and Georgia Department of Transportation (DOT), as well as technology companies, TomTom and Wejo. The infrastructure includes approximately 285 signalized intersections equipped with fisheye lens cameras that use computer vision for traffic detection, along with 214 Radar Detection Sensors (RDS) positioned about every half-mile that collect lane occupancy, speed, and vehicle count data every 30 seconds (Xu, Berres, et al. 2023). Traffic signal phase and timing data is collected every tenth of a second using the National Transportation Communications Protocol for Intelligent Transportation Systems (NTCIP) standard (Lakin 2021). Sanyal highlighted significant challenges inherent to working with legacy transportation systems. These include older controllers with unknown firmware versions, varying levels of connectivity (some standalone, others net- worked), and inconsistent settings across different controllers. The partial observability of current sensor networks creates gaps in coverage, particularly for sidewalks and broader area views, while maintenance issues and the high cost of upgrading to newer Lidar-based sensors present ongoing operational challenges. During the discussion, Sanyal addressed questions about weather impacts on sensor accuracy, cybersecurity vulner- abilities in industrial control systems, and the resistance of some manufacturers to protocol updates.
